document.title: Rumsfeld snowflake to Gen. Pace, "General McCaffrey's Report on Afghanistan," with McCaffrey report (June 3, 2006)
document.authors: Office of the Secretary of Defense (Donald Rumsfeld); attachment by Gen. Barry McCaffrey
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Afghanistan 20/20: The 20-Year War in 20 Documents | National Security Archive
document.note: [Secret] Rumsfeld recommends McCaffrey's assessment to Gen. Pace. The report notes rising violence and battalion-size Taliban engagements, urges nearly doubling the Afghan army, calls the police disastrous, and asks whether Pakistan is playing a double-cross, taking $1B/year while backing Taliban cross-border operations against India-related threats.

events.description: McCaffrey visits Afghanistan and Pakistan, meeting Afghan, US, NATO and Pakistani officials.
McCaffrey issues academic report on trip to West Point faculty.
Rumsfeld sends snowflake to Gen. Pace asking about Afghan small arms and force size, response due 14 July 2006.
NATO scheduled to assume total responsibility for Afghan battle space by February 2007.
Planned NATO assumption of total responsibility for Afghanistan's battle space.
McCaffrey report on Afghanistan dated.
McCaffrey assesses Pakistan, concluding Musharraf is not playing a deliberate double game and recommending border fencing and barriers.
Proposed completion target for a $1.2 billion project to connect province and district capitals to a unified national electricity grid.
McCaffrey concludes his report with recommendations for a 15-year US-Afghan cooperation strategy, reduced civilian casualties and higher priority for Afghanistan.
Taliban summer-fall campaign using battalion-sized units to knock NATO out, capture Kandahar and penetrate ANA/police.
McCaffrey met Pakistani officials and Pakistan National Defense College staff, including Gen Ahsan, MG Yusaf, LTG Raza and Dr. Mazari.
McCaffrey received briefings from US Embassy officers Grenik and Quinn and DEA's Tom Nuse.
NATO scheduled to assume total responsibility for the entire battle space of Afghanistan; next ISAF commander and HQ not yet identified.
Deadline (NLT Nov-Dec 2006) for the new NATO HQ to begin moving into Afghanistan.
NATO/ISAF scheduled to assume total responsibility for the entire battle space of Afghanistan; next ISAF commander and HQ not yet identified.
The new NATO HQ must begin movement into Afghanistan no later than Nov-Dec 2006.
ISAF takes OPCON of British, Canadian and Dutch NATO battalion combat teams.
Canadians engaged in fierce fighting with the Taliban, their first real combat exposure since WWII.
McCaffrey visit to Afghanistan and Pakistan (19-26 May 2006).
McCaffrey issued academic trip report memo to USMA Social Sciences dept.
Rumsfeld memo to Pace on McCaffrey's report, asking about small arms for Afghan forces and ANA size; response requested by July 14, 2006.
McCaffrey met Karzai with Ambassador and LTG Eikenberry.
McCaffrey visited 205th Corps in Kandahar.
McCaffrey recommends expanding the ANA/ANP to 70,000-100,000 troops within 18 months, funded at $1.2 billion annually for ten years.
McCaffrey assesses Pakistan's role. He does not believe Musharraf plays a double game and recommends considering fencing and barriers along the Afghan-Pakistan border.

sources_cited: Unclassified official US Government publications (human rights/narcotics reports)
Briefings by CFC-A, ISAF, JTF-76, Pakistani military and US Embassy officials
key_claims: The Taliban reconstituted in three years and now operate in battalion-sized units of 400+ men.
Taliban base areas in Pakistan are secure; Pakistan is an active sanctuary for the Taliban.
Drug money and international financial support have energized Taliban operations.
Taliban suicide bombers are not just foreigners, and show evidence of excellent training.
The Afghan National Army is severely under-equipped, with shoddy small arms.
Pakistani madrassas draw talented rural Afghan youths because of poverty and lack of schooling in Afghanistan.
NATO/ISAF faces vulnerabilities and must assume full battle-space responsibility by February 2007.
McCaffrey doubts Musharraf is playing a deliberate double game, arguing the Pakistan Army cannot be a dupe while suffering heavy FATA casualties.
He asserts the ISI, Frontier Police and much of Pakistan's state apparatus are effectively the Army.
He argues the Durand Line does not exist in practice and Pashtuns move freely between Quetta and Kandahar.
He states Pakistan controls only about 5% of Baluchistan and does not control most of FATA.
He recommends expanding the ANA and ANP to 70,000-100,000 and fencing selected border areas.
He warns NATO-ISAF is under-resourced and that the Taliban plan to target weak NATO contingents such as the Dutch.
